column3: Perform every act of thy life as if it were thy last.
Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores and mountains. But it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, ‘I have been harmed.’ Take away the complaint, and the harm is taken away.
Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.
Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
That which is a hindrance to action is turned to promote action, and that which is an obstacle on the road helps us on this road.
The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer.
Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
Thy present opinion founded on understanding, and thy present conduct directed to social good, and thy present disposition of contentment with everything which happens — that is enough.
No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
If it is not right, do not do it: if it is not true, do not say it.
Let it make no difference to thee whether thou art cold or warm, if thou art doing thy duty.
Remember that man lives only in the present, in this fleeting instant: all the rest of his life is either past and gone, or not yet revealed.
Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee.

Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.
It is a man's peculiar duty to love even those who wrong him.
There are more things likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
Nothing is ours, except time.
If a man knows not to what port he is steering, no wind is favourable to him.
As long as you live, keep learning how to live.
Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters.
Let us prepare our minds as if we had come to the very end of life. Let us postpone nothing.
Every day ought to be regulated as if it closed the series, as if it rounded out and completed our existence.
It is likely that some troubles will befall us; but it is not a present fact. How often has the unexpected happened! How often has the expected never come to pass!
Set aside now and then a few days during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, and shall say: ‘Is this the condition that I feared?’
It is equally faulty to trust everyone and to trust no one.
The greatest remedy for anger is delay.
It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it.
Everyone hurries his life on and suffers from a yearning for the future and a weariness of the present.
Fire is the test of gold; adversity, of strong men.
Behold a spectacle worthy of God: a brave man matched in conflict with evil fortune.
No man is good by chance. Virtue has to be learnt.
Cling to philosophy, that harbour which no storm can trouble.
Of things some are in our power, and others are not. Our opinions, movements, desires and aversions are in our power; our body, property, reputation and office are not.
Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.
Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
Remember that you must behave as at a banquet. Is anything brought round to you? Put out your hand and take a moderate share. Does it pass by you? Do not stop it.
Remember that you are an actor in a play, of such a kind as the author may choose. Your duty is to act well the part that is given you; to choose it belongs to another.
It is not he who reviles you or strikes you who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
Be silent for the most part, or, if you speak, say only what is necessary and in few words.
Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
On no occasion call yourself a philosopher. Sheep do not vomit up the grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten, but they digest the food inwardly.
The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is that he expects all advantage and all harm from himself.
Whatever rules are laid before you, abide by them as laws, as if you would be impious to transgress them.
I must die: must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains: must I then also lament? I must go into exile: does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness?
Difficulties are the things that show what men are.
Let death and exile, and all other things which appear terrible, be daily before your eyes, but chiefly death; and you will never entertain any abject thought, nor too eagerly covet anything.
You will fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.
He is free who lives as he wishes to live, who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance.
It is not poverty that causes sorrow, but covetous desires; and riches do not banish fear, but reasoning.
We have two ears and only one mouth, so that we may hear more and speak less.
Better to trip with the feet than with the tongue.
Well-being is attained by little and little, and nevertheless it is no little thing itself.
The end may be defined as life in accordance with nature.
Lead me, O Zeus, and thou, O Destiny, wherever your decrees have fixed my station. I follow cheerfully; and did I not, wicked and wretched, I must follow still.
Fate leads the willing and drags along the reluctant.
I have grown old, but I have not yet been made worse by it.
To live in accordance with virtue is the same as living in accordance with the experience of the things which happen by nature.
If I had followed the multitude, I should not have studied philosophy.
Nothing that happens in the universe happens in a manner contrary to reason.
